info.bio:
Crass  se formaron  en 1977 en Epping, Essex, inspirados por la primera oleada del punk, y tomándose en serio las proclamas vagamente políticas de los Sex Pistols. Los miembros del grupo vivían en una granja en comunidad, conforme a relaciones interpersonales cooperativas. Esta comunidad estaba formada por diez personas (músicos, técnicos y artistas de otras ramas) que lucharon por sus ideales con un grado de activismo muy alto.

scenes.name: Oi! y anarcopunk
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Las dos derivas del punk que se tomaron en serio la explotación y la injusticia social: el Oi! o «punk de verdad» (The Exploited, Cockney Rejects, Garry Bushell en Sounds como ideólogo), protesta extrema arraigada en la clase obrera, a veces contaminada por la ultraderecha; y el anarcopunk de Crass y su sello, discos-panfleto contra el Estado, la Iglesia y el Ejército, a favor del pacifismo y la autonomía. El gótico nació en parte como reacción contra su «temática mundana».

scenes.name: Punk-rock británico
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: La gira de los Ramones de 1976 contagia a Inglaterra, donde el punk es combinación de moda y paro: la Gran Bretaña de Thatcher, con las ciudades industriales devastadas, convierte el «punk» en algo mucho más serio que lo que pretendían los Ramones. Malcolm McLaren inventa el sonido (Sex Pistols, «los Ramones con heroína y valium») y la imagen. The Clash, los más intelectuales (London Calling, Sandinista); Damned, Generation X, Buzzcocks (inventores del punk-pop), Vibrators. En Australia, Radio Birdman y los Saints. La segunda ola (GBH, UK Subs, Neurotics, New Model Army, Stiff Little Fingers) y el punk anarquista (Crass, Discharge, Rudimentari Peni, Subhumans).

podcast.title: Falklands War Hoax Tape (1982)
podcast.body: Crass devised a prank in 1982 by editing speeches from Ronald Reagan and Margaret Thatcher to create a fake phone call that made it sound as if they were plotting a wider war against the Soviet Union, with Thatcher also appearing to take responsibility for the sinking of an Argentine battleship during the Falklands War. This idea stemmed from classified information shared by a former skinhead sailor who had served in the Falklands. Crass secretly sent the tape to newspapers across Europe. "Based on what they heard from this sailor, Crasse, who wrote it down, they took notes, came up with the idea of cutting together some speeches by Ronald Reagan and Margaret Fatcher to make it sound like a phone call between the two of them, sometime, allegedly, in 1982."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Great KGB Punk Rock Conspiracy

podcast.title: Invitation to Russian Literary Magazine (1982)
podcast.body: Shortly after their Falklands War hoax was uncovered in 1982, Crass was invited to a meeting at a supposed Russian literary magazine in London. This event, combined with subsequent approaches from various intelligence and radical groups, fueled suspicion within British intelligence about potential Soviet contact. "Crasse was invited to a meeting at a supposed Russian literary magazine in London."

podcast.title: "Thatchergate" Hoax (1983-1984)
podcast.body: Following the Falklands War, this anarchist musical collective created a tape known as "Thatchergate." They cobbled together speeches from Margaret Thatcher and Ronald Reagan to create what sounded like a fake phone call between the two leaders, including a fabricated discussion about firing missiles at allies. When the tape circulated in 1983, the US State Department suspected it was KGB disinformation, and MI6 considered it a possible Argentinian intelligence operation. Its true source was not discovered until January 1984. While not a song, its samples were used in tracks by Crass and the Dead Kennedys. Crass's motivation was to expose governments as "small-minded, petty and stupid," not just corrupt or violent, and the hoax indeed embarrassed the CIA. "The band cobbled together speeches from Margaret Thatcher and Ronald Reagan into what appeared to be a fake phone call between the two of them."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Anti-Establishment Stance & Thatcher Opposition
podcast.body: Crass was an anarchist punk collective that consistently challenged the establishment in all its forms, holding particular anger towards the policies of Margaret Thatcher. Their radical political leanings made them a subject of interest for both intelligence agencies and various subversive organizations. "They were particularly angry at the policies of Margaret Fatcher."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Courted by Subversive Organizations
podcast.body: Following the hoax, Crass was reportedly courted by various organizations, including the real KGB, Germany's Baader-Meinhof Group (Red Army Faction), and the IRA, who sought their assistance or information. The band members admitted to being terrified as their prank escalated into a situation they perceived as genuinely dangerous for themselves, their country, and the West. "Crafts started getting courted by all sorts of shitty organizations, including the real KGB."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Falklands Hoax Tape
podcast.body: Following an encounter with a sailor who divulged classified information from the Falklands War, Crass created a hoax tape in 1982. This tape, engineered from spliced speeches by Ronald Reagan and Margaret Thatcher, was designed to sound like a crossed phone call where they plotted a wider war against the Soviet Union, and Thatcher appeared to claim responsibility for sinking an Argentine battleship. Crass secretly sent the tape to newspapers across Europe as a joke. "Based on what they heard from this sailor, Crasse, who wrote it down, they took notes, came up with the idea of cutting together some speeches by Ronald Reagan and Margaret Fatcher to make it sound like a phone call between the two of them sometime, allegedly, in 1982."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Intelligence Agency Investigations and Harassment
podcast.body: After Crass's Falklands War hoax tape was uncovered, it triggered investigations by both the CIA and MI5, and the Pentagon also took notice. MI5 opened a secret dossier on the band, and their phones were tapped. The band was subsequently courted by various organizations, including the real KGB, Germany's Red Army Faction (Baader-Meinhof group), and the IRA, all expressing interest in their disruptive capabilities. Crass admitted to being terrified as their prank escalated into a genuinely dangerous situation involving national security. "MI5 opened a dossier on the band. It was kept secret for 30 years. The band had their phones tapped. Plus, intelligence spooks from the CIA looked at the tape and opened an investigation. The Pentagon took notice too."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Great KGB Punk Rock Conspiracy

podcast.title: Intelligence Investigations
podcast.body: After their hoax tape was discovered, Crass became the target of investigations by the CIA and MI5, who questioned if the band had contacts with Russian or Argentinian agents. MI5 opened a secret dossier on the band, kept for 30 years, and their phones were tapped, while the Pentagon also took notice of the incident. "For more than a year, the tape was discussed by both the CIA and MI5."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: KGB and Radical Group Courtship
podcast.body: Following their Falklands War hoax, Crass found themselves being approached by various organizations, including the actual KGB, representatives from Germany's Baader-Meinhof group, and even the IRA. These groups, seeing their potential for destabilization, sought to offer assistance or gather further information. Crass felt terrified as their prank turned into a serious national security concern. "Crasse started getting courted by all sorts of shitty organizations, including the real KGB."

xref.title: Band's Longevity
xref.body: Despite their initial "crass commercialism" and breaking up after their second album, Sigue Sigue Sputnik managed to survive "in fits and starts" over a period of 20 years, finally ending in 2004. "The band survived and fits and starts over 20 years, finally ending it all in 2004."

xref.title: Radio Ban in North America
xref.body: In North America, punk music, including The Ramones, faced significant resistance from radio stations due to its perceived political, class-oriented, crass, vulgar, and violent nature. "Radio stations wouldn't touch the Ramones."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 5: New Wave

xref.title: Used "Thatchergate" Samples
xref.body: The Dead Kennedys incorporated samples from Crass's infamous "Thatchergate" tape into their own musical tracks. This act connected them to a significant political hoax that fooled major intelligence agencies. "samples from this tape were used in tracks by both Crasse and the dead Kennedys."
